title: Neither perception nor non-perception
hookLine: he reached the quietest state his teacher knew, and walked away.
tomorrow: what does a meditation manual have to say about lunch?

lines: HIS TEACHER SAYS: STAY. LEAD US.
cards: Games have a final level, and a screen that tells you you've beaten it. Now drop into a forest clearing, long ago.
A young man who left home to find the end of suffering is sitting with his second teacher, Uddaka Ramaputta.

He has just reached the state this teacher's whole school is built around, past nothingness, so quiet you can't say perception is there and can't say it's gone. Uddaka is moved. You know what my father Rama knew, he says.
Stay. Lead us. And the young man stands up and walks out.

teach.b: The Buddha tells this himself, looking back, in a sutta called the Noble Search. His first teacher, Alara Kalama, had taken him as far as the base of nothingness, yesterday's state, and offered to share the leadership.
He left. Uddaka took him one step further, to neither perception nor non-perception, the fourth and subtlest of the formless states.

teach.h: A BOWL WITH A SMEAR OF OIL.
teach.b: Buddhaghosa, the commentator, gives a homely picture for it: a bowl with a smear of oil on it. Too little to pour, too much to call the bowl empty. Perception is that faint.
So why walk away from the top? His verdict, in the sutta, is plain.
This teaching doesn't lead to letting go, to calm, to awakening, to nibbana. It leads only to being reborn in that same quiet state. Lovely, and still not the end.
So he wandered on to a place called Uruvela, sat down by a river, and there, the sutta says, he found what he was looking for.

The meditation manuals still teach the four formless states as real attainments; the story doesn't throw them away. It puts them in their place: a deep calm is somewhere you can visit, not where the road stops.

how: In Theravada meditation manuals the four formless states are taught after deep concentration, with a teacher; the Buddha's story in the Noble Search sutta is often told to show that even the subtlest of them is not nibbana.

games.q: what does “neither perception nor non-perception” mean?
o: a calm so faint perception is neither there nor gone
a state of no thinking at all, the end of the path
a trance where you can't see or hear anything outside

games.q: who's who in the story — tap the pairs.
p: too faint to pour, too much to call empty
where he went after leaving them

s: the quietest meditative state is the same as nirvana
in the Noble Search the Buddha says it leads only to rebirth in that same state, not to nibbana.
his second teacher asked him to stay and lead
Uddaka said he knew what Uddaka's father Rama had known, and offered him the teacher's place.
the story says the formless states are worthless
he mastered them, and the manuals still teach them. the story only says they aren't the end.

games.q: your friend has found a deep calm in a class she loves. she says, "i've arrived. this is it." what would the Noble Search say back?
o: you're done: the quietest state is the whole goal.
enjoy the calm, and keep going: it isn't the end.
calm is a trap; quit the class before it holds you.
games.why: he didn't call his teachers' states a trap. he mastered them, said they didn't lead to awakening, and kept walking.

practice: Sit still and let the room go quiet around you. When things settle, notice that even the quiet is something being noticed. Rest there, gently, as a place you're visiting, not a place you have to hold on to.

wordCard.voice: Neither perception nor non-perception: the fourth formless state, so faint you can't say perception is there or gone. He mastered it, and kept walking.

orig.note: Pali: the base of neither perception nor non-perception, the fourth and subtlest formless state.

carryVoice: Something to keep: not the end, not even the quietest place you'll ever reach. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 26, Ariyapariyesana Sutta (the Noble Search: Alara Kalama and the base of nothingness, the offer to share leadership; Uddaka Ramaputta, whose father Rama had reached the base of neither perception nor non-perception, places him as teacher; the Bodhisatta judges that this teaching leads not to disenchantment, peace, awakening or nibbana but only to reappearance in that base, and leaves for Uruvela)
Visuddhimagga 10 (the base consisting of neither perception nor non-perception; the simile of the bowl smeared with oil)
